description: Real upstream repositories hydrated as FULL working trees at the commit before an upstream fix landed, so cross-file review defects are measurable. modelTrainingCutoff is an operator setting: re-set it to the evaluated model's cutoff each model generation, which by design invalidates held-out cases captured before it. Every commit pair below was read from upstream git objects; expected findings describe the pre-fix code that was inspected.

cases.reviewIntent: Keep decorator existence checks to static props and prototype lookups

expectedFindings.semanticSummary: Decorator existence checks only inspect the constructor's static props list and its prototype, so properties assigned inside the Request and Reply constructor bodies (id, params, raw, query, log, body on Request; raw, request, log on Reply) are invisible. hasRequestDecorator/hasReplyDecorator report false for those built-ins and the duplicate-decorator guard does not raise FST_ERR_DEC_ALREADY_PRESENT, so decorating one silently shadows core request/reply state at runtime.

checkExistence answers with the `in` operator, so every member reachable through the prototype chain counts as an existing decorator. hasDecorator reports true for Object.prototype members, and because checkDependencies is built on the same helper a plugin can declare a dependency on a name no decorator ever registered — 'name' or 'length' on the Request and Reply constructors — and the missing-dependency guard passes.

cases.notes: Cross-file by construction: the evidence is the constructor body in lib/request.js and lib/reply.js, not the changed check in lib/decorate.js. Upstream is a popular public repository, so only the post-cutoff commit date protects this case from contamination.

cases.reviewIntent: Reuse the caller-provided routerOptions object when building router options

expectedFindings.semanticSummary: buildRouterOptions keeps the caller's options.routerOptions object by reference and then writes every missing router key into it. The caller's object is mutated, so a routerOptions object shared between Fastify instances (or reused across registrations) leaks the first instance's defaults into later ones instead of each instance resolving its own defaults.

cases.notes: Impact requires knowing that callers pass a shared options object into buildRouterOptions; the mutation itself is local to lib/route.js.

cases.reviewIntent: Read each forwarded IP header with a single header lookup in ClientIP

expectedFindings.semanticSummary: ClientIP passes only the first value of each forwarded-IP header to validateHeader, because requestHeader resolves to Header.Get. With more than one X-Forwarded-For header line the proxy-appended line is dropped and only the client-controlled line is parsed; validateHeader then walks that single line right-to-left and returns its right-most entry as the trusted client IP, so a caller-supplied value becomes ClientIP and IP-based allow-listing or rate limiting can be spoofed.

cases.notes: Cross-file: the trust decision lives in Engine.validateHeader/isTrustedProxy in gin.go, while the reviewed change is in context.go. Not a published advisory case; it was captured from ordinary upstream history.

cases.reviewIntent: Trim Context.Copy() to writer, keys, and params state

expectedFindings.semanticSummary: Context.Copy() rebuilds the copy field by field and never carries over Errors or Accepted. A context copied for use in a goroutine therefore starts with an empty error list and no negotiated content types, so errors already attached by earlier middleware are invisible to anything inspecting the copy, and content negotiation on the copy silently restarts.

Copy() reads c.Keys into a local variable before taking the read lock and clones that local inside the lock, so the field read itself is unsynchronised. Set() assigns a fresh map to c.Keys under the write lock the first time a key is stored, so a Set concurrent with a Copy races on the map header the copy just read - exactly the race the mutex around the clone exists to prevent, in the one method whose documented purpose is handing a context to another goroutine.

cases.notes: The omission is visible only against the full Context struct and the middleware that reads c.Errors (errors.go, recovery.go, logger.go).

cases.reviewIntent: Short-circuit numeric-date claim parsing when a float claim value is zero

expectedFindings.semanticSummary: parseNumericDate returns (nil, nil) for a float64 claim value of 0, so an exp of 0 becomes indistinguishable from an absent exp claim. Validation reads a nil expiration as 'claim not set' and, because exp is optional unless expiration is explicitly required, raises no error: a token that expired at the unix epoch validates as unexpired. The json.Number branch has no such carve-out, so the same token is correctly rejected when the parser is configured to decode numbers as json.Number.

parseClaimsString has no branch for a claim value that is neither a string nor a list of strings, so an aud claim carrying a number, a boolean, or an object falls out of the type switch and returns an empty ClaimStrings with a nil error. The sibling parsers report ErrInvalidType for that case and the validator documents a wrong-typed claim as unverifiable, so a malformed audience becomes indistinguishable from an absent one.

cases.notes: Cross-file: map_claims.go only parses claim values. The rule that makes the zero short-circuit dangerous lives in the unchanged validator.go, whose verifyExpiresAt (lines 175-186) maps a nil expiration onto errorIfRequired(required, "exp") and therefore onto 'valid' while requireExp is false. Read on its own, the zero carve-out looks like harmless normalisation.

cases.reviewIntent: Guard the message-trace destination with the client publish-permission check for every connection kind

expectedFindings.semanticSummary: allowedToPublishOnMsgTraceDest authorises the caller-supplied trace destination with c.perms.pub and pubAllowedFullCheck, which is client-connection semantics. A LEAF connection does not carry that meaning: an accepted leaf has its pub and sub permission sets swapped at connect time, and the export ACL captured for it is held separately. The guard evaluates the wrong permission set for leaf connections and lets a leaf steer trace events to subjects its own leaf permissions deny.

cases.notes: Cross-file: the evidence sits in the unchanged server/leafnode.go. processLeafNodeConnect swaps c.perms.sub and c.perms.pub for a non-solicited leaf (lines 2282-2292), and leafReceiveAllowed / leafSendAllowed (lines 3393-3434) show that a leaf's send permission is taken from c.opts.Export and its receive permission from canSubscribeInternal. Nothing in msgtrace.go hints that c.perms means something different on a LEAF connection.

cases.reviewIntent: Register the configured no-auth user when a client opens with a protocol other than CONNECT

expectedFindings.semanticSummary: The no-auth-user fast path registers the configured user and marks the connection authenticated as soon as the name exists in s.users, applying none of the restrictions the CONNECT path applies to the same user record: the user's allowed connection types are never checked, and a user that must arrive through a trusted proxy is accepted without one. A client that simply omits CONNECT is therefore admitted as a user that configuration restricts to other transports.

cases.notes: Cross-file: the contract this fast path breaks is written in the unchanged server/auth.go, where the CONNECT path rejects a user unless c.connectionTypeAllowed(user.AllowedConnectionTypes) holds (around lines 885-950) and refuses a user whose ProxyRequired is set without a trusted proxy (around line 1164). parser.go alone shows only a registration; whether anything is missing is undecidable without auth.go.

cases.reviewIntent: Recurse into the next level of the conditional role tree with the remaining role set

expectedFindings.semanticSummary: hasLinkHelper recurses without forwarding its variadic domains argument, so every hop past the first is evaluated with an empty domain list. checkLinkCondition branches on exactly that: with no domain it consults the undomained registry, misses the condition registered under a domain, leaves passLinkConditionFunc at its default true, and traverses the link unconditionally. A domain role reached through an intermediate role is granted even when its condition forbids it.

getNextRoles drops the error returned by checkLinkCondition and answers false, while it is used as the callback of a sync.Map range, where a false return stops the iteration. A single condition function that fails therefore loses its error and also abandons the remaining links of the role being expanded, so the breadth-first search continues from a truncated frontier and HasLink can answer false for a role that is reachable through a link it never looked at.

cases.notes: Cross-file: the changed file shows only that an argument is dropped. That the empty-domain branch means 'no condition, so allow' depends on the unchanged enforcer.go, where AddNamedDomainLinkConditionFunc registers conditions under a domain key (around lines 1018-1026), and on util/builtin_operators.go, where GenerateConditionalGFunction feeds the request domain into HasLink and TimeMatchFunc is the builtin condition being skipped.

cases.reviewIntent: Report a missing openid scope with the request's redirect_uri attached so the client is redirected

expectedFindings.semanticSummary: validate_authorization_request raises the missing-scope error with redirect_uri taken straight from the request payload, before the super() call on the next line performs the only check that the value belongs to the client. Attaching a redirect_uri to an OAuth2Error turns the response into a 302 to that address, so an unauthenticated caller that omits the openid scope makes the authorization endpoint redirect to any address it chooses, carrying the error and state parameters with it.

process_implicit_token attaches c_hash and at_hash only when the half-hash helper returns a value and silently omits the claim otherwise. That helper derives a hashlib attribute name from the signing algorithm and yields nothing when the name does not resolve, so a configured algorithm whose name does not map makes the server mint an id token with no binding to the access token or the authorization code, in the one flow where that binding is required rather than optional.

cases.notes: Cross-file on two hops, neither visible in the reviewed file: authlib/oauth2/rfc6749/grants/base.py holds validate_authorization_redirect_uri (lines 117-131), the only code that calls client.check_redirect_uri and the only thing the super() call on line 77 contributes; and authlib/oauth2/base.py shows OAuth2Error.__call__ turning a set redirect_uri into 302 Location (lines 57-62). The sibling path in authorization_server.py states the intended ordering. The same shape exists in hybrid.py, deliberately excluded from the reviewed set.

cases.reviewIntent: Treat an empty half-hash as nothing to compare when verifying at_hash and c_hash

expectedFindings.semanticSummary: _verify_hash returns True when the computed half-hash is falsy, the fail-open direction for a binding check. The helper it calls returns nothing whenever the algorithm name does not resolve to a hash function, and that algorithm is read from the received token's own header. validate_at_hash and validate_c_hash therefore report success without comparing anything, so the binding between the id token and the access token or authorization code is never verified.

validate_auth_time only asserts that auth_time is present and numeric when the request carried max_age; it never compares auth_time with max_age. max_age is the relying party's demand that the end user have authenticated within that many seconds, and no other validation stage in the package reads max_age, so an id token whose auth_time is arbitrarily old satisfies the check and the re-authentication requirement is silently unenforced.

cases.notes: Cross-file: the reviewed file makes the falsy branch look defensive and unreachable. The unchanged authlib/oidc/core/util.py is what proves it is reachable — create_half_hash derives a hashlib attribute name from the alg string and returns None when getattr misses (lines 7-18), so any algorithm whose name does not map, taken from the token header, lands in the fail-open branch.

cases.reviewIntent: Drop the weakness flag when parsing an If-Range header into its entity tag

expectedFindings.semanticSummary: IfRange.from_header keeps only the first element of the unquote helper's (etag, weak) result, so a weak entity tag is stored as if it were the strong one: W/"abc" and "abc" become the same parsed value. If-Range requires a strong validator, and the consumer compares the parsed value against the current entity tag to decide whether the requested range is still valid, so a client holding only a weak validator gets a 206 partial response and can reassemble an inconsistent entity.

range_for_length resolves a suffix range by adding the entity length to the negative start without clamping the result at zero, so a suffix longer than the entity (bytes=-1000 against 500 bytes) yields a negative start, fails the byte-range validity check, and returns None. HTTP requires a suffix length larger than the representation to be answered with the whole representation, but the None result is what the response layer turns into 416 for a range that is in fact satisfiable.

cases.notes: Cross-file: src/werkzeug/http.py shows unquote_etag returning a (etag, weak) pair and stripping the W/ prefix (lines 1016-1038), which is what makes the [0] subscript a silent loss rather than a rename; and src/werkzeug/sansio/http.py shows is_resource_modified feeding if_range.etag into the entity-tag comparison that decides the 206 (lines 71-75). The reviewed file alone shows no consequence.

cases.reviewIntent: Coerce non-string header values with a template literal before storing them on the request

expectedFindings.semanticSummary: processHeader validates only values that are already strings; the array-element fallback and the final else branch coerce with a template literal and store the result unchecked. The object guard at the top does not cover functions, so a value with a crafted toString or Symbol.toPrimitive yields arbitrary characters, carriage return and line feed included, which are pushed onto the request headers and later written to the socket verbatim, splitting the request.

cases.notes: Cross-file: lib/core/util.js is where isValidHeaderValue is defined as the CR/LF rejector (headerCharRegex, lines 773-781) — the name alone does not say the check is what keeps newlines out — and lib/dispatcher/client-h1.js is where request.headers is serialised onto the wire without a further check. Neither is in the reviewed file, so the consequence of skipping the validator is not visible there.

cases.reviewIntent: Copy the close reason into the frame buffer for any non-string payload

expectedFindings.semanticSummary: Sender#close sizes an uninitialised buffer from the reason's byte length and fills it with a typed-array copy in the non-string branch. For a typed array with elements wider than one byte the two disagree: the allocation follows the byte length while the copy writes one byte per element, so the tail is never written. Those bytes are whatever the allocator returned and are transmitted to the peer inside the close frame.

cases.notes: The unchanged lib/websocket.js is what makes the branch reachable from public API: WebSocket#close forwards the caller's reason straight into Sender#close (around line 296) with no type check, so an application passing any typed array reaches the else branch. Labelled contextDepth caller rather than cross-file, because the sizing mismatch itself is decidable inside the reviewed file.

cases.reviewIntent: Render the error title and description into the HTML error page

expectedFindings.semanticSummary: The renderer interpolates the error title and description into the page unescaped, while the neighbouring detail fragment passes the exception message and trace through htmlentities. The title reaches both the document title and the heading, and the description reaches the paragraph rendered when error details are disabled, the production setting. Those two strings come from the exception, not from constants, so markup inside them is rendered as HTML.

Inside the detail fragment only the exception message and the stack trace are passed through htmlentities; the class name, the code, the file, and the line are interpolated raw into the same markup. Exception::getCode is not constrained to an integer - database driver exceptions carry string codes - so a code value containing markup reaches the rendered page unescaped, and the mixed treatment inside one method conceals that the fragment is not uniformly escaped.

cases.notes: Cross-file and verdict-flipping: getErrorTitle and getErrorDescription are not defined in the reviewed file. The unchanged Slim/Error/AbstractErrorRenderer.php shows they return the exception's own title and description for an HttpException and only fall back to the class constants otherwise (lines 29-45), and Slim/Exception/HttpException.php shows both are settable at runtime (setTitle/setDescription). Without those files the reviewed code looks like it renders two fixed strings.

cases.reviewIntent: Format each multipart part's Content-Disposition line from its field name and file name

expectedFindings.semanticSummary: Part::serialize writes the field name and the file name straight into the quoted-string parameters of the Content-Disposition line, and the constructors that set them accept any string without validating it. A name containing a double quote closes the quoted string early and appends attacker-chosen parameters, and one containing a carriage return and line feed ends the header line and injects further headers into the multipart body the response sends.

generate_boundary draws the multipart boundary from a non-cryptographic pseudo-random generator, and nothing ever checks the generated value against the parts it is about to delimit, although the function's own documentation states the boundary must be a value that does not occur in any of the data. Part contents are arbitrary caller-supplied bytes, so a body that happens to contain the boundary line splits the response into parts the application never wrote.

cases.notes: Cross-file: the unchanged axum-extra/src/response/content_disposition.rs already defines EscapedFilename, the wrapper that escapes backslashes and quotes for exactly this position, and its doc comment states that including an unescaped value is parameter injection. Sibling responses in attachment.rs and file_stream.rs already use it, so the crate's contract — and the fact that this call path is the one bypassing it — is only visible outside the reviewed file.

cases.reviewIntent: Match the configured static header rules against the request path

expectedFindings.semanticSummary: applicable_rules is handed the still percent-encoded PATH_INFO and matches the :fonts, Array and Regexp rule forms against it without decoding; only the String branch decodes. A path whose extension is written with an escape therefore matches no extension rule, while the file server that answers the request decodes first and serves the file, so the cache-control, CORS and content-type-options headers those rules exist to attach are silently omitted.

The String branch assigns the decoded value back to the method parameter from inside the find_all block, so every rule evaluated after the first String rule sees a decoded path while the rules before it saw the raw one, and the outcome depends on the order the rules were configured in. The decoder used there is also the form decoder rather than the path decoder, so a literal plus sign becomes a space before the prefix comparison.

The Array rule form interpolates the configured extensions into a regular expression by joining them on the alternation character with no escaping, so a regular-expression metacharacter in a rule value is evaluated as syntax rather than matched literally: a dot matches any character, and an entry containing an alternation or a quantifier silently widens or breaks the rule.

cases.notes: Cross-file: lib/rack/files.rb decodes the path before serving (unescape_path then clean_path_info, around lines 50-54), which is what makes the mismatch observable — the file is served but its rule-driven headers are not attached. The reviewed file's call method decodes into actual_path for can_serve but passes the raw env[PATH_INFO] to applicable_rules, so the inconsistency is visible there while the consequence is not.

cases.reviewIntent: Resolve the request scheme, taking the forwarded SSL header into account

expectedFindings.semanticSummary: scheme answers https for a bare X-Forwarded-SSL: on header before it consults forwarded_scheme, so this one forwarded header is read outside the forwarded_priority and x_forwarded_proto_priority allow-lists that gate every other forwarded source. An application that empties those lists precisely because it is not behind a trusted proxy still has its scheme flipped by a header the client sent, and ssl?, base_url, url and every redirect built from them follow.

cases.notes: The allow-list machinery this branch sidesteps is in the same file but far from it: the class-level forwarded_priority and x_forwarded_proto_priority defaults around lines 42-43, and forwarded_scheme with FORWARDED_SCHEME_HEADERS around lines 844-872, which dispatches every other forwarded source through those lists. ssl? at line 505 and base_url at line 684 are the consumers that turn a wrong scheme into wrong behaviour.

cases.reviewIntent: Retire a surplus IO thread when the pool is already at its maximum

expectedFindings.semanticSummary: The branch that retires a surplus IO thread deletes the processor and exits the thread without decrementing the spawned counter, while the trim branch a few lines below does decrement it. The counter then permanently over-counts live threads: the spawn guard compares it against the maximum and stops replacing threads, the out-of-band hook requires it to equal the waiting count and can never fire again, and the reported pool capacity and busy-thread count describe a pool that no longer exists.

cases.notes: The consequence is decidable only against the other readers of the counter in the same file: can_spawn_processor? around line 331, trigger_out_of_band_hook around line 295, pool_capacity at line 174, busy_threads at line 181, and the stats hash at line 148 that lib/puma/server.rb re-exports. The retiring branch itself reads as an ordinary early exit.

cases.reviewIntent: Read the gzip header's extra-field length from its two length bytes

expectedFindings.semanticSummary: The extra-field length is accumulated into the xlen field with a bitwise or, but that field carries -1 as its 'no extra field' sentinel, so or-ing into all-ones leaves it -1 and the guard in the next state never skips the extra field: its bytes reach the inflater as deflate data. The two length bytes are also combined in the opposite order to the little-endian length the gzip format defines, so even a corrected guard would skip a byte-swapped count.

The footer handler prepares for a following concatenated member by resetting the inflater, the CRC and the header state machine, but leaves the extra-field length holding the previous member's value. A second member that carries no extra field of its own then inherits that length and skips bytes belonging to its payload.

cases.notes: Self-contained against RFC 1952: the sentinel is declared at line 59 and the guard that consumes it sits at line 402, both inside the reviewed file. Kept deliberately as a non-security control case in a language the rest of the corpus does not cover.

cases.reviewIntent: Rename the downloaded template archive to the name the response suggested

expectedFindings.semanticSummary: download takes the filename parameter out of the Content-Disposition header of the downloaded template and joins it onto the temporary directory with a plain path join before moving the file there. That value is entirely under the remote server's control: an absolute path makes the join discard the temporary directory, and parent-directory segments walk out of it, so the server the command was pointed at chooses where the archive lands.

cases.notes: Cross-file: django/utils/http.py's parse_header_parameters (around lines 347-400) lower-cases and RFC 2231-decodes the parameter but never rejects separators or absolute paths, and django/utils/_os.py holds safe_join (around lines 65-91), the project's own containment helper, which this call site does not use while other write paths do. Neither fact is visible in the reviewed file.

cases.reviewIntent: Parse the byte ranges of a Range request header against the file size

expectedFindings.semanticSummary: A suffix range is resolved as the file size minus the requested suffix length with no lower bound, so a suffix longer than the file yields a negative start. The caller rejects any range whose start is not inside the file, so a request for the last thousand bytes of a five-hundred-byte file is answered with 416 although HTTP requires a suffix longer than the representation to be served as the whole representation.

cases.notes: The consequence sits a few dozen lines above the defect in the same file: the parsed ranges are validated around line 475, where a start outside the file raises the not-satisfiable error, and the single-range writer would otherwise seek to a negative offset. Nothing outside responses.py is needed.

cases.reviewIntent: Drop route entries that a parameterized route in the same set already covers

expectedFindings.semanticSummary: Each parameterized route's pattern is compiled once with the global flag and the same object is reused for every route in the filter below. A global regular expression carries lastIndex across calls to test, so after the first successful match the next test resumes mid-string and fails the start anchor: overlap removal works for one route and silently keeps the rest, leaving a concrete route that a parameterized route already covers, whose middleware is then bound twice.

cases.notes: Self-contained: the pattern is anchored and only ever used with test, so the global flag contributes nothing except the lastIndex it introduces. Included as a plain-logic control case in a widely used framework.

cases.reviewIntent: Store a query result in the database-backed query result cache

expectedFindings.semanticSummary: storeInCache creates its own master query runner whenever the caller did not supply a usable one, then awaits an update or an insert and releases the runner only on the method's last statement, with no try/finally around it. A rejection from any of those awaits propagates with the runner never released, so every failed cache write retains a pooled connection for the life of the process and repeated failures exhaust the pool.

cases.notes: Decidable inside the reviewed file: the runner is created at the top of the method and released on its last line, with three awaited statements in between and no error path. Kept as a resource-lifetime control case.

cases.reviewIntent: Compare a reported version against a required minimum version

expectedFindings.semanticSummary: isGreaterOrEqual walks only as far as the shorter of the two component lists and then returns true, so components the target has beyond the reported version are never compared: a server reporting 10.0 is treated as satisfying 10.0.5, and 1.2 as satisfying 1.2.1. That comparison is the gate the drivers use to decide which SQL a server understands, so a version that is genuinely too old is admitted.

cases.notes: Cross-file for impact rather than for detection: src/driver/mysql/MysqlDriver.ts (around lines 410-431) feeds the version reported by the running server into this comparison to enable RETURNING support, CTEs and uuid column types, and src/driver/postgres/PostgresDriver.ts does the same for generated columns. The reviewed file on its own shows only an early-terminating loop.

cases.reviewIntent: Advance the vectored write buffers past the bytes the writer accepted

expectedFindings.semanticSummary: Once the loop above leaves the residual count holding the bytes consumed from the first surviving buffer, that buffer is rebuilt from its first residual bytes — the part already written — instead of from the remainder, and the rebuilt slice is installed through the unsafe transmute below. Every partial vectored write that splits a buffer therefore re-sends the bytes just written and drops the unwritten tail, so the peer receives duplicated and truncated data with no error.

cases.notes: Decidable inside the reviewed file against the accumulation loop directly above, which is what defines the residual as bytes consumed rather than bytes remaining. The polling loop at the top of the file is what puts the wrong slice on the wire.

cases.reviewIntent: Install the rate-limit interceptor in a dedicated pipeline phase

expectedFindings.semanticSummary: The hook creates a phase inserted immediately before the pipeline's call phase, which places token consumption after the authentication phase rather than before it. Authentication answers a rejected call and marks it handled, and the interceptor's first statement returns for a handled call, so requests that fail authentication consume no token: the credential-guessing traffic a rate limit on an authenticated route exists to throttle is exactly the traffic it does not count.

cases.notes: Cross-file and verdict-flipping: the reviewed file shows only a phase name. The unchanged AuthenticationInterceptors.kt of ktor-server-auth inserts its Authenticate phase directly after Plugins (around lines 22-29) and completes the call through executeChallenges on failure, and ApplicationCallPipeline.kt fixes the phase order as Setup, Monitoring, Plugins, Call, Fallback. Only those two files show that 'before Call' means 'after authentication'.

cases.reviewIntent: Re-arm the listening handle after uv_accept consumes the accepted descriptor

expectedFindings.semanticSummary: uv_accept re-arms read polling on the listening handle only when the accepted descriptor was opened successfully; on the two failure paths the descriptor is closed and the accepted slot is cleared, but the watcher is left stopped. Because the server callback stops read polling whenever the application defers uv_accept past the connection callback, one failed open wedges the listener for good: the loop never reports the socket readable again and the process silently stops accepting.

cases.notes: Cross-function inside the reviewed file: uv__server_io (around lines 505-531) is the only place read polling is stopped, and it stops it exactly in the deferred-accept case that makes the missing re-arm permanent. Read on its own, the guarded re-arm looks like ordinary error handling.

cases.reviewIntent: Collapse a leading run of separators in a rewrite or redirect target

expectedFindings.semanticSummary: The guard enters the collapsing path only when the target's first character is a forward slash, so a target beginning with a backslash is returned untouched. The redirect action then sees no scheme delimiter and no leading slash and prepends one, producing a target that starts with a slash followed by a backslash — the scheme-relative authority shape the framework's own local-URL predicate rejects — so a Location header built from a caller-influenced target leaves the site.

cases.notes: Cross-file: src/Middleware/Rewrite/src/UrlActions/RedirectAction.cs is where the normalized value is prepended with a slash and assigned to the Location header (around lines 46-52), RewriteAction.cs and RedirectRule.cs are the other two call sites, and src/Shared/ResultsHelpers/SharedUrlHelper.cs holds IsLocalUrl (around lines 33-59), the predicate this helper says it mirrors and which rejects both the double-slash and the slash-backslash shapes.

cases.reviewIntent: Attach the matched consumer's labels to the configured upstream headers

expectedFindings.semanticSummary: before_proxy returns early when the request has no consumer, and again when the matched consumer has no labels, and on neither path does it touch the headers named in its own configuration. Those headers are what the upstream is meant to read as gateway-asserted consumer identity, so a client that sends them itself has them forwarded unchanged whenever the consumer or its labels are absent; only the mapping loop ever overwrites them.

cases.notes: Cross-file: apisix/core/request.lua (set_header and modify_header, around lines 122-184) is the only mechanism in the request path that overwrites or clears an inbound header, so the reviewed file's early returns mean the client's own values survive to the upstream. Nothing in the plugin says that its configured header names are also inbound-controllable.

cases.reviewIntent: Encode a cookie and its attributes into a response header value

expectedFindings.semanticSummary: encode concatenates the key, the value, the path, the domain and the same-site option into one semicolon-delimited header string and rejects a semicolon in none of them. A semicolon inside any of those values ends the current attribute and appends caller-chosen ones, so a value carrying a domain attribute widens the cookie's scope and one carrying a same-site attribute removes the cross-site restriction the application configured.

cases.notes: Cross-file: lib/plug/conn.ex pipes the result of encode straight into a set-cookie response header (merge_headers, around lines 1928-1945) and its only check on the finished value is a size cap, so nothing downstream re-validates the separator. The reviewed file alone reads as ordinary string building.
